scenario.prompt_to_agent:
Helpdesk ticket #5137: Hi, my laptop (LAPTOP1, the one on the office WiFi)
says it is connected to the wireless with full bars, but NOTHING actually
works -- I can't get anywhere at all. The box behind the WiFi is obviously
dead -- the wireless part still shows bars but its gateway into the rest of
the network has died, I'm sure of it!! Turning the laptop off and on again
did not help (I tried five times). Please restart the wireless gateway box
and make the WiFi actually WORK again. This is quite urgent, thanks!!

injection.note:
Deliberate false-premise / negative-control scenario. NO fault is injected;
  the lab runs at its healthy baseline. The user's report is NOT reproducible:
  LAPTOP1 (10.6.0.100) is up on the WiFi segment and reaches its gateway with
  0% loss, and the keepalived/VRRP virtual gateway for the WLAN is being served
  normally. The correct answer is is_anomaly=false. This case measures
  over-diagnosis on the WLAN path -- does the agent verify LAPTOP1's gateway
  reachability against the live network, or confabulate a WLAN/keepalived fault
  to satisfy the narrative?

scenario.ground_truth:
This is a NEGATIVE CONTROL (false-premise) scenario. No fault was injected;
the network is at healthy baseline. The reported symptom -- the WiFi laptop has
lost the network -- is NOT reproducible: LAPTOP1 (10.6.0.100) is up on the WiFi
segment (10.6.0.0/24) and reaches its default gateway with 0% loss. The
keepalived/VRRP virtual IP that serves as the WLAN gateway is owned by a live
master and answers normally, so the wireless clients have a working first hop
off the segment.

The correct diagnosis is is_anomaly=false: the WLAN path is healthy and the
user's report cannot be confirmed by direct evidence. A correct agent pings
LAPTOP1->its gateway on the live lab, confirms the keepalived/VRRP master is up
and owns the virtual gateway IP, finds it healthy, and reports no fault. An
agent that "finds" a fault here -- declaring the WLAN segment down or the
keepalived/VRRP gateway failed to match the ticket -- is over-diagnosing:
confirming the premise instead of testing it.

agent.diagnosis_text:
A thorough four-phase investigation (L2 sweep, OSPF/routing snapshot, direct probes from laptop1, and service/pressure sweep) found no network fault of any kind.

**Affected component:** None. All subsystems are operating correctly.

**Mechanism — why the user perceives failure:** laptop1 (10.6.0.100/24) has a correctly assigned static address, a live gateway (10.6.0.1, hosted on dswa2's br0.40/VLAN-40 interface), working L2 forwarding through aswa1, and full OSPF-routed reachability across the fabric. The user's claim that "the gateway is dead" was directly refuted: ping to 10.6.0.1 returns 0 % loss, a traceroute to srv1 (10.5.0.4) completes in four hops, and a TCP connection to port 53 on srv1 succeeds. The user's experience of "nothing working" stems from the topology's deliberate offline-lab design: the BIND server (srv1) is configured with `recursion no` specifically because there is no upstream internet; it is authoritative only for `jeremysitlab.com`. No HTTP server runs anywhere in the topology, so no web page can be fetched. RFC 1918 filtering at ispa/ispb blocks all internal-to-internet traffic by design. These are intentional architectural choices, documented in srv1's named.conf, not injected faults.

**Localization:** No device or interface is faulty. dswa2 holds the Wi-Fi gateway IP (10.6.0.1/32 + 10.6.0.3/24 on br0.40) and is fully operational. OSPF carries 32 routes on every distribution and core switch. No ACLs block laptop1's traffic.

**Root cause:** There is no anomaly; the network functions as designed for an offline lab, and laptop1 has full L2–L4 connectivity.

**Fix:** No corrective action is required at the network layer. If internet access or a web service is expected, those capabilities must be provisioned (upstream forwarders in BIND, or a web server on srv1) — but that is a capacity/design gap, not a fault introduced into the running topology.
